title: Interpreting transverse and longitudinal wave graphs
prior_knowledge_summary: A progressive wave transfers energy while particles oscillate locally about equilibrium.
In a transverse wave particle displacement is perpendicular to energy transfer, while in a longitudinal wave it is parallel.
Compressions have particles closer together and rarefactions have particles farther apart.
new_learning: Interpret displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs without treating either as a literal path.
Translate between a longitudinal particle pattern and a displacement-distance graph.
not_yet_taught: wave intensity, power per unit area and intensity-amplitude relationships

blocks.heading: One curve, two very different questions
content: A smooth curve is drawn on a graph. Is it the shape of a rope across the room, or the motion of one rope point through time? The curve alone cannot tell us.
Before reading any wave graph, read both axes. The horizontal axis decides what the curve means.

figure.purpose: Create the central graph-reading puzzle by showing identical curves with different horizontal axes.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with two identical sinusoidal curves side by side. Label both vertical axes displacement. Label one horizontal axis distance and the other time. Add a question bubble asking same curve, same meaning?
figure.alt_text: Two identical curves have distance and time as different horizontal axes.

blocks.heading: A displacement-distance graph is one instant
content: A displacement-distance graph is a snapshot of many particles at the same instant. Choose a position on the horizontal axis and the graph gives the displacement of the particle at that position.
For a transverse wave, the vertical graph value can match the physical up or down displacement. Even then, the curve is a set of particle displacements, not the route followed by one particle.
The distance between consecutive points in the same state of oscillation is one wavelength. A crest-to-crest spacing on a transverse displacement-distance graph is one example.

figure.purpose: Connect a transverse displacement-distance snapshot to individual particle displacements and wavelength.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper paired sketch. Above, a rope snapshot with several coloured points. Below, a displacement-distance graph at one instant with matching coloured points, equilibrium line, amplitude and one wavelength. Use sparse arrows from rope points to graph points.
figure.alt_text: A rope snapshot maps many particle displacements onto a displacement-distance graph.

blocks.heading: A displacement-time graph follows one position
content: A displacement-time graph follows one chosen particle or position while time passes. Every point on the curve belongs to that same location in the medium at a different time.
The greatest magnitude of displacement is the amplitude. The time between consecutive identical states of motion is the period.
Think of a camera fixed on one coloured rope marker. Its record through time is a displacement-time graph. This is different from taking one photograph of the whole rope.

figure.purpose: Contrast a fixed-position time record with the many-position distance snapshot.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper sequence with one coloured rope marker shown at five successive times, then a displacement-time graph beneath. Mark amplitude and one period. Include a small camera icon fixed at one position.
figure.alt_text: One rope marker at successive times produces a displacement-time graph.

blocks.heading: Use slope to find motion direction
content: Suppose a transverse profile travels to the right without changing shape. A small time later, the entire profile is shifted slightly right.

At a point where the profile slopes upward to the right, the part of the profile arriving from the left has a lower displacement. The particle therefore moves downward. Where the profile slopes downward to the right, the arriving part is higher, so the particle moves upward.
This is a comparison of two nearby snapshots. Do not use the graph height alone: height gives displacement, while the local slope and travel direction reveal the immediate motion direction.

figure.purpose: Teach motion direction from two nearby right-travelling snapshots without a memorised sign rule.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper overlay of an initial transverse profile and the same profile shifted a small distance right. Highlight one rising-slope point with a downward motion arrow and one falling-slope point with an upward motion arrow. Keep the two snapshots in different colours.
figure.alt_text: A right-shifted wave profile shows downward motion on a rising slope and upward motion on a falling slope.

blocks.heading: A longitudinal wave can also have a smooth displacement graph
content: For a longitudinal wave, the graph's vertical direction is only a value scale. A positive value can mean displacement to the right and a negative value displacement to the left. The particles still move parallel to wave travel.
Imagine particles initially equally spaced. Move each particle right or left by the amount shown on a displacement-distance graph. The new spacing reveals compressions and rarefactions.

A compression forms where displacement becomes more negative as distance increases. Neighbouring particles are shifted toward one another. A rarefaction forms where displacement becomes more positive as distance increases, so neighbouring particles spread apart.

figure.purpose: Translate a longitudinal displacement-distance curve into an actual particle-spacing pattern.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper three-row construction. Row 1 shows equally spaced equilibrium particles. Row 2 shows a displacement-distance curve with positive meaning right and negative meaning left. Row 3 shows displaced particles, with one negative-gradient compression and one positive-gradient rarefaction labelled.
figure.alt_text: A longitudinal displacement graph maps equal particle positions into compressed and spread-out regions.

blocks.heading: A peak is not automatically a compression
content: It feels natural to label the top of a longitudinal displacement graph as a compression because it looks like a crest. That shortcut fails because graph height gives particle displacement, not particle spacing.

At a maximum or minimum of displacement, the local slope is zero, so neighbouring displacements are momentarily changing very little with position. Maximum compression and rarefaction occur near zero-displacement crossings where the slope has its greatest magnitude.
Read the slope: negative slope means compression and positive slope means rarefaction. Then return to the physical particle pattern to check whether spacing really decreases or increases.

figure.purpose: Correct the peak-equals-compression misconception using graph slope and particle spacing.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper misconception panel. Cross out compression written at a displacement peak. Mark a negative-slope zero crossing linked to crowded particles and a positive-slope zero crossing linked to spread particles. Add the short cue read slope, then check spacing.
figure.alt_text: Compression matches a negative graph slope, not simply a displacement peak.

blocks.heading: Read every wave graph in three moves
content: First read the axes. Distance means many positions at one instant; time means one position at many instants.
Second read the value. Height gives displacement. Spacing along a distance axis can give wavelength, and spacing along a time axis can give period.

Third connect the graph to the wave type. For a transverse wave, displacement is perpendicular to energy transfer. For a longitudinal wave, the plotted vertical height is only a displacement value, and the slope translates into particle crowding or spreading.
A graph is a representation of measurements. It is not automatically the path of the wave or the shape of the medium.

figure.purpose: Consolidate the axis-value-physics routine for both wave types.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map with three boxes: read axes, read value, connect to physical wave. Branch distance to snapshot and wavelength, time to one-position record and period, then branch transverse to physical displacement and longitudinal to slope and spacing.
figure.alt_text: A decision map links graph axes and values to transverse and longitudinal wave physics.

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch
visual_planning.boundary_note: Figures teach graph interpretation only. They do not introduce intensity or any later topic.

concepts_taught: displacement-distance graph as a simultaneous spatial snapshot
motion direction from a travelling transverse profile
longitudinal displacement gradient as particle crowding or spreading
misconceptions_addressed: A wave graph always shows the physical path or shape of the medium.
A peak on a longitudinal displacement graph is a compression.
Graph height alone gives the immediate direction of particle motion.
next_lesson_can_assume: Distinguish displacement-distance from displacement-time graphs by their axes.
Read amplitude, wavelength and period from the appropriate representation.
Translate a longitudinal displacement-distance graph into compressions and rarefactions using slope.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Use intensity as power per unit area.
Use any relationship between intensity and amplitude.
Apply Doppler, polarisation or superposition ideas.
